So‚ the following interview was conducted with Pat Irwin on behalf of the Georgia Dental summer map for Grinnell concerts‚ Georgia Dental and student life in History and Memory Project. It took place on August 2‚ 2024 on WebEx. And the interviewer is myself‚ Hayden Suarez- Davis‚ so we have the legal release that's all signed and confirmed. So let's just get into let's get into the interview. So if you could start Pat by just introducing yourself‚ you know your name‚ your class‚ year‚ where do you live now? And what are you up to?

Hello. This is Pat Irwin. I'm Grinnell‚ class of 1977. I live in New York City‚ which is where I am at the moment‚ in a neighborhood called Long Island City. I'm looking at the 59th Street Bridge through the alley here. I'm a musician and composer‚ and I've been working in New York City since the late 70s.
Perfect. Okay‚ so

just going back to you know‚ your Grinnell experience‚ what did you dowhen you were at Grinnell? What did you study? And if you you know‚ is‚ was there a professor or a class that really stands out when you think about your time at Grinnell?
Well‚ I was an American Studies major. I particularly remember Professors‚ Alan Jones‚ Richard Cleaver‚ both stick out in my mind‚ and
I was very interested in oral history.

I believe I had a seminar with Professor Wall‚ Joe Wall as well‚ but I had an independent oral history project of my own when I was a Grinnell student. But most notably‚ I was concert chairman and worked with Georgia Dental.
Right? And that's a perfect segue into this‚ into this next‚ next question. You know‚ if you could describe sort of your main extracurricular activities at Grinnell.

Well‚ one of my favorite activities was we had a choir‚ which we called the celestial‚ celestial sacred harp singers. And that was a group of friends that basically got together and sang hymns out of the it's known as the‚ traditional sacred harp hymnal. We did that on our own and gave concerts and performed at Herrick chapel and other places. If I remember correctly‚ that was my main extracurricular activity. I don't think I had too many others.
I don't recall.
Of course‚ concerts chair‚ you know?
And of course‚ that was a fairly time consuming.
Yeah‚ definitely can relate to that. How would you describe‚ sort of the general like‚ student atmosphere‚ student culture during your time at Grinnell?

Well‚ I treasure it. I mean‚ I lived off campus my senior year‚ and perhaps I was— went to Grinnell in London my junior year. Both of those experiences really were impactful. I mean‚ I lived it on High Street. I believe 809‚ High Street. And then my senior year‚ I lived on a farm in Malcolm‚
so that was way off campus.

And I just remember the wonderful‚ collegial atmosphere. Concerts‚ of course‚ were transformative events‚ mind blowing‚ mind expanding‚ thrilling experiences where we‚ you know‚ brought phenomenal music and musicians to the campus. Movies‚ of course. I just love the general liberal arts atmosphere‚ and— the access we had to our professors was remarkable. And really the access to each other living in the dorms‚ whether it was North or South Campus‚ and I‚ you know‚ formed friendships that I still have to this day.
Right? And so you said you lived off campus your senior year‚ right? You lived on campus your senior year—
Both‚ both the second half of my junior year and senior year.
Gotcha. And so when you lived on campus‚ you know‚ freshman and sophomore‚ where did you live?
I lived in Reed Hall‚
my first year‚ and Younker my second year.
Perfect. Okay‚
yeah. So now‚ if we could just now‚ let's move on to the main topic‚ Georgia. So could you just sort of tell me about your first interaction‚ your first impression with Georgia.
I don't think I really remember my first impression‚

but I remember basically having a relationship with her that was completely based on being on the phone. I never met her until many years later‚ and she was a voice on the other end of the phone. I would see her at concerts‚ so I knew what she looked like‚ but it was mostly‚ well‚ it was totally on the phone.

Right? Yeah‚ I know we had a lot of‚ we‚ we've had some‚ you know‚ done some other interviews‚ and a lot of people have mentioned‚ you know‚ some of them‚ you know‚ especially in the in the 80s or whatever‚ they didn't even know what she looked like until they saw pictures of her‚ or whatever‚ just‚ you know‚ being on the phone I think. And‚ so going off of that‚ you know‚ what was it like working? What was it like working with her and organizing shows?

Well‚ she was the one with the experience‚ and I and my concert CO‚ concert chairperson‚ Dan Hexter‚ we were the ones with the ideas. But she knew how to make things work. She knew what budgets were. She knew what a booking agent was. She knew what routing meant. We were just fans. So‚ you know I would safely say we were clueless‚ and until we‚ you know‚ began to work with Georgia. And she would‚basically tell us what a certain Act would cost‚ what it would take to get to Grinnell‚ that type of thing. You know‚ she was our advisor‚ and she was a good advisor.

Right? And‚ so you guys would go to her with like ideas in‚ you know‚ like you were essentially suggesting‚ you know‚ you were saying‚ I want to book this particular act. And then she would tell you if it was viable or not. And then she would do sort of the work on negotiating the price. Is that what you're saying?
Yes.
Right‚ okay‚ and that was all done over the phone‚ right?

Right.

Okay‚ so‚ is there a concert or an event that you‚ that you worked on— or actually‚ I'm going to go back a little bit. When you were‚ you know‚ she was— you said you saw her at the at the shows‚ sometimes. Could you explain a little bit like‚ what were you involved with when it came to the shows? Like‚ would you help set up? Would you help sort of transport the band? Like‚ what were you involved with that she sort of set up the background‚ but then you carried out? I guess‚ if that makes any sense.

First of all‚ she was pretty hands off when it came to that. We had to kind of figure it out. Well‚ you know‚ we weren't completely on our own‚ but we had to figure it out. There was some set up‚ some tear down involved. I remember driving to the Cedar Rapids airport to pick up Bill Evans and his band‚ the great piano player. Other acts would arrive on their own‚ you know‚ with their own transportation.
You know‚ just depends on how things were routed.
Right‚ so‚ she was involved with the booking aspect‚ but when it came to the actual‚ like‚ running of the shows‚ you said she was pretty hands off in that sense.
Totally‚ yeah.

Right. Okay‚ yeah that makes sense. And then‚ you know‚ you talked about Bill Evans‚ is there sort of another concert or another event that you‚ like‚ really remember or really cherish during your time at Grinnell?
Oh! Many.

Charles Mingus was transform— that was phenomenal. I still think about it to this day. Bill Evans‚ mainly for that car ride. Asleep at the Wheel‚ I remember. I'm still in touch with them‚ you know‚ I ran into the bass player from that band recently. That was fun‚ and he remembered the gig. It was his first show with the band. The Persuasions came to my house on‚ well— I just forgot‚ I lived on Main Street for a while too. They they came to my house on Main Street after the show‚ and we stayed up all night singing. That was fun. You know‚ each one had its own little unique personality. You know‚ this was‚ like a big deal‚ just to see that kind of entertainment‚ world class stuff.
Right? And‚ you know‚ a big deal in the sense of just the location‚ is what you're saying? You know‚ the location being‚ a rural area.

Well... no‚ I wouldn't put it that way. And as a matter of fact‚ now that I'm a working musician‚ that's— I wouldn't put it that way. No‚ it was just the proximity I had to‚ basically working musicians. You know‚ I got to talk to these guys. I got to meet them. I you know‚ it wasn't deep‚ but they were working musicians. And this was something that was very interesting to me.
Right? Yeah‚ that makes sense.

I mean‚ when I think about something like that‚ I think of the famous— like Herbie Hancock jamming with Duke Ellington and his band when they were‚ when Duke was performing here‚ right? When Herbie was a student. I mean‚ I think it's just the‚ you know‚ if you're really interested in music‚ it's the proximity of just sort of having access to this really incredible musicianship that can really be transformative‚ and sort of make you think‚ you know‚ make you think about what you want to do‚ or sort of inspire you.
Right? Okay‚
Okay. Yeah‚ so this is kind of a two part question‚ I'll ask the first one‚ first. How did other students feel about sort of the general social program at the time?
I think‚ generally speaking‚ it was a very positive program.
I mean‚ very positive experience. It was crucial.
It was essential to the campus life.

And‚ the arts in general‚ I think are crucial to education anyway. But you know‚ we tried to be sympathetic to a variety of tastes‚ and try to accommodate as many as possible. In retrospect‚ I think we could have been done a lot better‚ but I think we did pretty well.

Yeah‚ and‚ you know‚ there's obviously the concerts and the films aspect‚ and so there's like‚ there wasn't really this sense of‚ “oh‚ you know‚ there's nothing to do or whatever.“ There was always‚ people always people always felt like there was stuff due on the weekends?
Oh‚ yeah.

Okay‚ perfect. And so then‚ you know‚ going off of that just specifically related to Georgia. How did other students or faculty or staff for that matter‚ perceive Georgia and her contributions‚ as someone who tended to speak over the phone and was a little bit in the background‚ if you will?
I don't think too many people were aware of her.
So not‚
not many people were aware of her‚ okay‚ that makes sense.

column3: Okay‚ so basically‚ you know‚ she stayed in the background‚ and then her job was in jeopardy‚ and then people just sort of came out of the woodwork and were like‚ “This person is important‚“ essentially‚ is what you're saying?
I wouldn't quite put it that way. No‚ I'm fact‚ not at all.
But we did lobby the student body‚ as well as the faculty‚ to‚ you know‚ sort of speak out on her behalf. And we‚ we got a lot of traction there.
Right. Okay‚

and so let's see‚ you sort of touched on this. But‚ you know‚ were there any other like controversies or incidents surrounding Georgia and the administration‚ or was it really just the conflict with her position at the time?
Yeah‚ I don't think there was‚
any sort of‚ like‚ conflict.
You know‚ I'm sure she had to advocate for our budget‚ but—
and we were sort of aware of that‚
—but it didn't dominate our discussions at all.
It wasn't‚ like I said‚
until she was in danger of losing her job‚ that that she became more of a presence. Not physically‚ but people just became more aware of who she was.
Right? And then‚ you know‚ actually‚ this is a great segway to the next question‚ which is‚ how were concerts and student life in general impacted by the college's financial situation at the time?

Well‚ we had to —and this is where one thing that Georgia was just masterful at— we had to basically work within a budget. So if we wanted to have a balance of concerts throughout the year‚ each semester‚ we needed a budget for each one. And she was very‚ very‚ very‚ very conscious of that‚ and directed that.

And so‚ you know‚ obviously there was a juxtaposition between‚ I guess like‚ you know‚ potentially bringing in a really popular band‚ but blowing all the budget for one show‚ versus sort of stacking concerts in between the year with like‚ you know‚ relatively less popular bands. Is that what you're saying?
Yeah. I mean‚ we just basically had to‚
budget.

So‚ you know‚ we learned what Acts were more economical‚ what bands. Georgia would have contacts with various agencies who knew what bands or acts would be touring‚ which allows for more economic‚ you know‚ greater economy. Rather than doing a one off‚ flying a band in from New York or wherever they live is not particularly economical‚ but grabbing a band while they're on tour is a‚ you know‚ much more economical way to go.

Right? I feel like that's‚ you know‚ that's one of the things that I've definitely learned over the past couple years. But also‚ I think it's‚ you know‚ obviously important to have those connections‚ right? Like you can't really do the routing‚ if you don't have the connections to the agents. And that's where I feel like I've heard that she was really successful in that regard. Just sort of a follow up on that‚ you talked about‚ you know‚ which genres or which bands were economical. I read the the Billboard magazine piece that they did on Georgia and Grinnell concerts‚ I believe it was in 1975. And‚ one of the things that they said was that we were pretty well known for sort of straying outside of the Rock and Roll dichotomy‚ also bringing in‚ like jazz and blues artists. I was wondering if that is sort of related to this idea of‚ were jazz and blues artists more economical or less expensive than rock and roll artists during your time there?

Well‚ I would put it more —that is not inaccurate— but I would prefer to say it would be more pop artists. There would be‚ certainly some jazz artists who would be out of our range as well. But yeah‚ pop‚ generally speaking‚ pop and rock acts have a higher price tag.
Yeah‚ right‚ okay‚ perfect‚ and I think so‚ we got through all that.
So could you talk a little bit about just how your interactions with Georgia‚ sort of impacted your life? Post-Grinnell.
Well‚ we stayed in touch.

And she kept in touch with— I'm a musician. She booked my band‚ or somebody booked my band after‚ or one of my bands in there. I don't remember the year‚ but I mean‚ it was just all part of the the process for me to become a working musician. I mean‚ she kind of laid out the foundation. I'm in a very DIY type band right now. We just finished a tour. We played Nashville‚ Louisville‚ Nelsonville festival in Ohio‚ as well as Chicago. And you know‚ some of the things that I learned at Grinnell are still with me now.
The basics haven't changed.
Yeah‚ I just‚ I just looked it up at our event list. Was this‚ I think you know‚ if you were talking about the the Raybeats‚ I believe it was?
It looks like that was in May of 1981 does that sound familiar?
Yeah‚ I'll be damned. Sounds about right.

Yeah‚ May of 1981. Yeah‚ one of the things I've been doing this semester is essentially putting together a list of events that have happened at Grinnell. And so I'm excited for people to be able to‚ you know‚ go to the website and be like‚ “oh‚ you know‚ I was here in‚ you know‚ from 1982 to 1986‚ I remember the show‚“ or whatnot that they may have forgotten about. So‚ yeah‚ that's been‚ that's been really fun. I mean‚ I think it's interesting. It's interesting‚ sort of what you're saying on the drawing aspect of the basics haven't changed. I was just talking with an alum recently from the early 2000s and that was one of the things that he said‚ where it was like being able to just sort of talk to musicians‚ and being‚ you know‚ being a concerts chair‚ booking bands‚ doing all this stuff‚ he still uses a lot of those‚ a lot of the things that he learned‚ a lot of experiences today‚ and it seems like you're sort of saying a different thing. But what I find interesting is you're saying it from a from a more musicians perspective‚ where he's saying it from an agent's perspective. So I think it's just interesting the— I don't know‚ like the range of experiences that people can‚ you know‚ that a similar role or similar title‚ if you will‚ can sort of impact different‚ like job outcomes‚ I guess.
Right. Yeah‚ you know. I mean‚ I just‚

it's the life. I mean‚ you‚ you unders— you learn‚ you know‚ seeing Charles Mingus lead his band‚ or Hound Dog Taylor showing up‚ you know. And those gigs are just as important as any other gig‚ you know? You give it all you've got‚ and you show up on time‚ you hit it‚ you quit it‚ we move on to the next one. And that can be anything from‚ you know‚ my first B-52's tour was 18 months long. You know‚ you learn to pace yourself. And‚ when you get to see great‚ great musicians in action‚ it's unforgettable. The way they act with one another‚ the way they do— what a sound check is! Just seeing Gil Scott Heron do a sound check‚ making the set list up beforehand‚ or doing it on the bandstand‚ just little‚ tiny things. I mean‚ it all adds up.

No‚ yeah‚ totally. I mean‚ yeah‚ that I feel like‚ just just doing concerts for the past couple years‚ I feel like I can definitely‚ you know‚ definitely relate to that‚ just like being able to— for me‚ it's sort of like being able to sort of see the results of the work that you did‚ I guess is‚ is also kind of‚ you know‚ rewarding‚ I guess‚ in that sense. But‚ yeah‚ no‚ I think that totally makes sense. So if I remember‚ if I'm remembering correctly‚ the Mingus‚ the Charles Mingus show‚ that was in the forum‚ right?
Yeah.
But there was something about‚ like‚ if I remember correctly‚ it was‚ ideally‚ it would not have been in the forum? I believe.
I'm sorry‚ what's that?
So‚ like‚ ideally‚ it would have been in Roberts or something like that‚ or‚ I don't know if—
I don't remember anything about that. I remember being in the north lounge‚ and it was tight. But I don't remember anything with regards to that.

Gotcha‚ yeah. And then just in the forum. Could you— you know‚ because we see the forum right now as‚ it's the computer services and‚ like‚ Student Health and Wellness building. So I was just wondering if you could talk a little bit about the forum‚ when it was hosting events and whatnot.

Well‚ there were‚ there was the North lounge and the South lounge. And some concerts were in the north‚ some were in the south‚ and they were‚ you know‚ Hound Dog Taylor‚ for instance‚ was in the south lounge‚ and it was a sweaty dance. Rocking. The smaller— you know‚ the North lounge was Mingus‚ The Persuasions. I remember Byron Browers‚ autoharp player. You know‚ it was like a coffee house in the north lounge. We sat on the floor‚ it was very‚ very intimate‚

Yeah. I mean‚ I've heard a lot of really‚ really awesome stories‚ and it's just interesting to think about‚ you know‚ like I said‚ because literally‚ now it's the building‚ essentially‚ where‚ as a student‚ I go in if I'm sick or if I need help with a computer. So it's very funny to hear‚ sort of all these stories of shows or whatnot in there. Okay‚ yeah. So‚ I think‚ you know‚ I'm pretty good on all my follow ups. Just wondering‚ is there anything that you would like to add to this that we didn't specifically cover?
Well‚ I mean‚ generally speaking‚ I think of the concerts as an essential part of my liberal arts education.
Crucial.

And‚ every bit as important as a political science class or English literature‚ American literature‚ creative writing‚ and I hope it continues to be a vital part of campus life. I feel passionate about it right now as a working musician‚
also that it's just... just essential.
And‚ I'm thrilled to have had the experience that I had while at Grinnell. It's priceless. It was priceless. And staying in touch with Georgia after I graduated was really wonderful.
You know‚ she kept tabs on me and we stayed in touch. That was fun.

And would you say that your classmates —even those who weren't necessarily as involved with concerts as you were— do you think they feel the same about‚ you know‚ it being an essential part of their like‚ liberal arts experience?
